title: Names, objects and mutation
summary: Why y = x does not copy a list, and how mutation differs from rebinding.
prereqText: You should be able to write loops and functions in Python. Lists and append are used without introduction.

blocks.html: You are cleaning survey data. You write raw = [4, 5, 3], then clean = raw so you can "keep the original", and then you fix a typo with clean.append(2). Later you print raw and the 2 is there too. Nothing in the code looks like it touched raw. This lesson explains that behaviour, and gives you a method to predict it every time.

blocks.prompt:
Before reading any explanation, predict what this prints.
x = [1, 2, 3]
y = x
y.append(4)
print(x)
options: An error, because y is not a list

feedback.0: This treats y as a separate copy made at the moment of y = x. That is the most common misconception: assignment does not copy a list.
feedback.2: append adds to the end of a list; it does not replace the contents.
feedback.3: y is bound to the very same list object as x, so y is a list and append works.

blocks.explanation: y = x binds the name y to the object x already refers to. There is only one list, so appending through y is visible through x. [source]

blocks.html: Think of a Python variable as a sticky label attached to an object, not as a box that contains a value. y = x sticks a second label on the object that already carries the label x. Changing the object changes it for everyone who reads it by either label.
blocks.limits: The label picture hides two details: labels belong to a namespace (a function has its own labels), and some objects (numbers, strings, tuples) cannot be changed at all, so for them a second label never causes surprises. Also, an object can carry many labels, or none, in which case Python may discard it.

blocks.purpose: Show that assignment and mutation act on one shared object, while an expression like x + [5] builds a new object.
blocks.alt: Left diagram: names x and y each have an arrow to one shared list object [1, 2, 3, 4]. Right diagram: name z has an arrow to a separate new list [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. This shows that y = x shares one object, whereas x + [5] creates a new one.

blocks.title: References, identity and mutability
blocks.html:
In Python an assignment such as y = x binds a name to an object. Every object has an identity that never changes during its life, and the is operator compares identities [data model 3.1]. Here is the official explanation of our opening puzzle: doing y = x does not create a copy of the list; it creates a new variable that refers to the same object [FAQ].

Whether a shared object can surprise you depends on whether it is mutable. Objects whose value can change are mutable, and those whose value cannot change are immutable. Numbers, strings and tuples are immutable; lists and dictionaries are mutable [data model 3.1]. So two names sharing an int is harmless: there is no way to change that int.

Two operations are easy to confuse:

  • Mutation changes the object in place (y.append(4), y[0] = 9). Every name bound to that object sees it.
  • Rebinding moves one name to a different object (y = [9], y = y + [5]). Other names stay where they were.

The trickiest case is augmented assignment. The language reference says x += 1 is similar to x = x + 1 but not exactly equal, and that when possible the operation is performed in place, modifying the old object [7.2.1]. For lists, s += t extends s with the contents of t [sequence types]. So x += [6] mutates the list, while x = x + [6] rebinds x to a new list. Simplification: "when possible" is the language definition; for the built-in list it is always in place, which is what I verified by running the code below.

a = [1, 2]; b = a; a = a + [3]
print(a, b)        # [1, 2, 3] [1, 2]      rebinding

p = [1, 2]; q = p; p += [3]
print(p, q, p is q) # [1, 2, 3] [1, 2, 3] True   in-place

Not verified: the sentence 'a = 1; b = 1 may or may not share an object' is implementation-dependent per the data model, so never use is to compare values; use it only to ask 'is this the same object?'.

blocks.title: Trace: which names see which change?
blocks.html:
We trace this program line by line, writing down which object each name points to. The final output is from a local python3 run.

x = [1, 2, 3]
y = x
y.append(4)
z = x + [5]
x += [6]
print(x, y, z)

steps.html: A list object L1 = [1, 2, 3] is created; x points to L1.
y is bound to the object x points to: y -> L1. No new list exists.
Mutation of L1, which is now [1, 2, 3, 4]. Both x and y show it.
+ on lists builds a new list L2 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; z -> L2. L1 is untouched.
In-place extension of L1, now [1, 2, 3, 4, 6]. y sees it as well; z (L2) does not.
Line 6 prints [1, 2, 3, 4, 6] [1, 2, 3, 4, 6] [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Check: x and y show the same list because they are one object; z differs.

blocks.result: Method: for every line decide mutation (object changes, all names see it) or rebinding/new object (only one name moves).

predict.prompt: After line 3, what does x show?
predict.explanation: x and y name the same object, so the append is visible through x.

predict.prompt: Does line 4 change what x shows?
options: No, z is a new list
predict.explanation: x + [5] builds a new list; no existing object is mutated.

steps.title: In-place +=
steps.html: += on a list mutates L1, so y changes too.

predict.prompt: After x += [6], what does y show?
predict.explanation: += extends the list in place, and y is the same list.

blocks.instructions: Answer each prediction before moving on, and say aloud whether the line mutates an object or rebinds a name.
blocks.debrief: You should have noticed that only lines 3 and 5 mutate, that line 4 creates a new object, and that the in-place += behaves unlike x = x + [6].

blocks.task:
Predict the output, then check it by running the code in your own Python 3 (the page cannot run it):

a = [10, 20]
b = a
b = b + [30]
c = a
c += [40]
print(a, b, c)
hints: Which lines mutate the list that a points to, and which create a new object?
b = b + [30] rebinds b. c += [40] extends the object c shares with a.
rubric: I identified that b ends up on a new list
I identified that a and c are the same object
My prediction matched my local run, or I found out why not
blocks.solution: b + [30] is a new list, so b = [10, 20, 30] and a is not changed by it. c is the same object as a; c += [40] extends it in place. Result: [10, 20, 40] [10, 20, 30] [10, 20, 40] (my local python3 3.14.5 run agrees).

blocks.task: Write, in your own Python file, a 5-line program in which exactly two of three names share one list and the third is independent, and where printing all three shows the difference. Predict the output before running it, and use is to confirm which names share an object.
rubric: Exactly two names are the same object (confirmed with is)
One name is an independent list
The prediction was written before running
I can state if each change was mutation or rebinding
blocks.model:
a = [1]
b = a
c = [1]
b.append(2)
print(a, b, c)
print(a is b, a is c)

Expected [1, 2] [1, 2] [1] and True False. I ran this locally and got exactly that.
blocks.externalFeedback: Your own interpreter is the judge: compare your prediction with the real output and explain any difference.

questions.prompt: After p = [1]; q = p; p = [2], what is q?

feedback.1: This assumes that rebinding p moves q too. Rebinding changes only the name p.
feedback.2: Nothing was appended; p was pointed at a new list.
feedback.3: q still points at the original list.

questions.explanation: p = [2] rebinds p to a new object. q still points to [1]. I confirmed this locally (output [9] [1, 2] for the analogous case).

questions.prompt: Which statement mutates the list that both names share (assume a = [1]; b = a)?

feedback.0: + builds a new list and rebinds b.
feedback.2: A new list literal; b moves.
feedback.3: list(b) creates a new list; this is a copy.

questions.explanation: += on a list extends it in place [sequence types].

questions.prompt: Why is s = 'ab'; t = s; t += 'c' safe for s?
options: Strings are immutable, so += makes a new string and rebinds t
t and s are different from the start

feedback.1: Assignment never copies; here sharing is harmless because the object cannot change.
feedback.2: It works; s stays 'ab', t is 'abc' (local run).
feedback.3: They share the same object until t is rebound.

questions.explanation: Immutable objects cannot be changed in place, so the operation must create a new object [data model 3.1].

questions.prompt: In your own words: what is the difference between mutation and rebinding?
rubric: Mutation changes the object, visible via every name
questions.model: Mutation changes an existing object (append, item assignment, +=), so all names bound to it see the change. Rebinding points one name at another object (=, x = x + ...), leaving other names alone.

blocks.task: A colleague's pipeline: defaults = [0.1, 0.2]; then model_a_params = defaults, model_b_params = defaults; later model_b_params[0] = 0.9, and model A now trains with 0.9. Explain exactly why, name the kind of operation involved, and give two different one-line fixes.
rubric: Explains both names refer to one list
Names the item assignment as mutation
Gives a valid fix: copy such as list(defaults) / defaults.copy() / defaults[:]
Gives a second distinct fix, e.g. separate literals or a function returning a fresh list
blocks.model: Both names point to the same list object; model_b_params[0] = 0.9 mutates it, so A sees it. Fixes: model_b_params = defaults.copy(), or model_b_params = [0.1, 0.2] built separately (or a function def make(): return [0.1, 0.2]). A shallow copy suffices because the items are floats (immutable).
